originalRequest: Author a complete English course for the open Agent-courses site, slug learn-brief-an-agent, for a reader who can get an agent running but whose output is frequently 'not what I asked for'. Terminal task: rewrite one real, vague request into a brief carrying acceptance criteria, then run an agent task with it end to end. Five lessons on underspecification, why agents proceed silently instead of asking, acceptance criteria before implementation, examples beating adjectives, and negative boundaries. Not a prompt-tricks listicle: stay on stating the requirement so the agent cannot build the wrong thing. Do not re-teach delegation basics (agent-first-real-task lessons 1-2) and do not enter SKILL.md or reusable-workflow territory (agent-skills-reuse).
learnerBrief: The reader has already delegated successfully at least once: they can hand an agent a task, watch it run, and read what came back. Their problem is upstream of operation. Runs complete cleanly and produce something they did not want, and their working theory is that they need better phrasing — which sends them to prompt-technique lists that do not address the actual defect. The defect is that their requests contain decisions they never noticed making, the agent fills those decisions silently, and nothing in the output marks which parts were invented. The course has to build the habit of finding those decisions and stating them, without assuming the reader can read code, and without teaching a product surface that will be renamed within two quarters.

briefCompleteness.evidence: The request named the target reader (can run an agent, output is frequently not what was asked for), the terminal artifact (one real vague request rewritten as a brief with acceptance criteria, then run end to end), the five lesson themes in order, and three explicit exclusions (not a prompt-tricks listicle, no delegation basics, no SKILL.md territory). The course-matrix design doc at docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-23-course-matrix-design.md entry L1-2 supplied the ladder position and the adjacent-course boundaries. The predecessor course learn-agent-first-real-task ends by naming this course's territory — 'if your runs complete but produce the wrong thing, the problem is upstream in how the task was specified' — which fixed the seam. Nothing about the audience or objective had to be guessed.
briefCompleteness.sourceNote: Written in a non-interactive run; no clarifying questions were asked because none were needed.

learnerModel.targetReader: Someone who has had an agent complete real work for them, and who keeps getting results that answer a recognizable version of their request but not the one they meant.
knownConcepts: Handing a task to an agent and letting it run
Reading an agent's summary and judging whether the result is what they wanted
Navigating their own project files and opening a text editor
Recognizing, in their own domain, when finished work is wrong
unknownConcepts: Programming in any language, and reading code
Writing formal specifications, user stories, or requirements documents
Test frameworks, assertions, and what a test suite proves
Agent Skills, SKILL.md, and skill packaging
Prompt-engineering technique vocabulary (few-shot, chain-of-thought, system prompts)
Benchmark methodology and how to read a research result
learnerModel.assumedEnvironment: Their own computer, their own project or files, and one agent tool of their choice that can read and write locally. The course assumes nothing about which tool, provides no sandbox, runs nothing on their behalf, and never asks them to upload anything. Lessons 1 through 4 need only a text editor; only Lesson 5's Level 2 exercise requires an actual run.
learnerModel.firstIndependentAction: Take one request they sent an agent in the last two weeks that came back wrong, list what it did not say, and mark each item recoverable, leave-to-agent, or state-it — a paper exercise needing only a text editor and their own memory of the run.
noviceRamp: Lesson 1 opens on an experience the reader has already had (a run that succeeded and produced the wrong thing) and introduces underspecification as a property of their own request rather than as a research term to learn.

The two research sources are introduced through their findings, not their methods: the reader is never asked to interpret a benchmark, and the one numeric claim carries its experimental setting in the same paragraph.

Every term follows everyday handle to visible example to formal name: 'something the agent can find by looking' precedes recoverable blank, 'a choice with more than one defensible answer' precedes decision blank, 'a specific choice the agent produced' precedes invented value, 'what must not happen' precedes negative boundary.

Acceptance criteria are taught without test vocabulary. The worked examples check row counts, timings, file diffs, and observable page states — things the reader can verify by looking — and the one criterion that mentions a test suite is used to demonstrate why that criterion is weak.

Examples across the course are drawn from mixed domains (invoices, onboarding emails, analytics events, a settings page, a payment flow) so a non-programmer can participate in every worked example, and code appears only as short illustrative snippets never required for the argument.

Exercises escalate from paper-only in Lessons 1 and 4, to a no-work agent exchange in Lesson 2, to a graded run in Lesson 3, to the full assembled brief and end-to-end run in Lesson 5. The first real run never happens before the reader has criteria to grade it against.

scope: Covers how to state a requirement so an agent cannot build the wrong thing: finding the decisions a request left blank and sorting them from what the agent can discover itself; why an agent fills a blank rather than asking, and what makes it ask; writing acceptance criteria that are checkable without the author's judgment, before implementation, with evidence attached; replacing evaluative adjectives with reference patterns and varied examples; and choosing the few negative boundaries that earn their place, each with its reason. Ends with the reader assembling a six-part brief and running one real task with it. Deliberately excludes: prompt-technique catalogues and phrasing tricks; delegation basics, task boundaries, action trails, and when to interrupt, which belong to the preceding course agent-first-real-task; SKILL.md, packaging, and reusable workflow files, which belong to agent-skills-reuse; repository-level instruction files such as AGENTS.md; context management on long runs; verification gates beyond the criteria written into a brief; and any programming instruction.

evidence: Ambig-SWE (arXiv 2502.13069), v3 revised 2026-02-21, accepted at ICLR 2026; PDF fetched and read in full during this session: supplies the detection finding, the non-interactive default, the 74% figure with its three experimental conditions, and the question-quality finding.

Learning to Ask (arXiv 2409.00557), EMNLP 2025, v4 revised 2026-04-29; PDF fetched and read during this session: supplies the next-token-prediction mechanism and the 56.0% Instructions Missing Key Information figure from 1,000 annotated real user instructions.

Anthropic 'Prompting best practices' (platform.claude.com), fetched 2026-08-23: covers the Claude 5 model family explicitly, supplying the colleague test, the example-selection rules and the 3-5 count, the reasons-generalize principle, the scope-limiting prompt, and the irreversible/visible-to-others action classes.

Anthropic 'Prompting Claude Opus 5', fetched 2026-08-23: supplies the current scope-expansion behaviour and the literal-instruction-following caution, both stamped in Lesson 5 prose as an as-of-date snapshot.

Anthropic 'Best practices for Claude Code', fetched 2026-08-23: supplies the 'Claude stops when the work looks done' mechanism, the evidence-over-assertion rule, the before/after prompt pairs, the interview workflow, and the trust-then-verify gap.

Anthropic 'Harness design for long-running application development' (published 2026-03-24), fetched 2026-08-23: supplies the sprint contract, the 27-criteria granularity, the self-evaluation finding, and the gradable-criteria move for subjective targets.
OpenAI 'Prompting' (learn.chatgpt.com), fetched 2026-08-23: supplies the Goal/Context/Output/Boundaries frame and the boundary-budget guidance, as an independent second-vendor framing.

GitHub 'Best practices for using GitHub Copilot to work on tasks', fetched 2026-08-23: supplies acceptance criteria as a named component of a well-formed task from a third vendor, and the semantic-code-search point that grounds the recoverable/decision split.
topicCurrency.staleRisk: The scope-expansion and over-verification behaviours in Lesson 5 and Lesson 3 are model-specific as of 2026-08-23 and are the first thing here that will age; Lesson 5 says so in its own prose and states that a more literal future model would make those boundary lines wasted rather than load-bearing. The Ambig-SWE 74% figure is a point-in-time upper bound over a model set that already includes superseded models (Claude Sonnet 3.5, Llama 3.1 70B, Deepseek-v2), and is taught with its three conditions and its variance across models attached; if it is re-measured on current models, Lesson 2's numeric paragraph should be updated rather than the argument, which rests on the direction. The five documentation pages (Claude Code best practices, Anthropic prompting best practices, Prompting Claude Opus 5, define-success/develop-tests, OpenAI prompting, GitHub Copilot best practices) are versioned rather than dated and are recorded in sources.md as retrieved 2026-08-23; the Anthropic prompting page in particular is organized around a named model list that will change. The Goal/Context/Output/Boundaries vocabulary is one vendor's current framing and may be renamed; the course uses it as a named frame with attribution rather than as universal terminology. The next-token-prediction mechanism in Lesson 2 is the most durable claim in the course and is not expected to move.
topicCurrency.competitorDelta: The competing site treats this material as prompt technique. This course refuses the listicle framing: every technique here is tied to a documented failure mechanism (silent value invention, self-assessment leniency, scope expansion) and every claim about what agents do today comes from a source opened during this session. Where a durable design principle is cited from older material, the prose says so.

qualitySelfReview.diagramUse: One mermaid diagram in the whole course, in Lesson 1: a two-question filter routing an unstated thing to recoverable, let-it-choose, or state-it. It earns its place because the material is a decision procedure with two sequential tests and three outcomes, and prose kept flattening it into a list that lost the ordering — the first question has to be asked before the second is meaningful. Nothing else in the course was drawn. Lesson 3's checkable-criteria material and Lesson 4's criterion-versus-example comparison are tables instead, because both are lookups across independent rows with no structure to trace. Lesson 5's three-question boundary sort is deliberately a plain-text table rather than a diagram, because the reader is meant to copy its columns into their own scratch file and fill them in, which a rendered SVG does not support. No decorative diagram was added anywhere.
weakestPoints: The outline came pre-set from the course-matrix design doc (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-23-course-matrix-design.md, entry L1-2) and was NOT individually human-confirmed before prose was written, because this was an unattended run. The five themes, their order, the target reader, the terminal task, and the exclusions are all as specified there. What no human validated is whether this is the right decomposition — in particular whether examples-versus-adjectives (Lesson 4) deserves a full lesson or belongs inside the acceptance-criteria lesson, and whether the silent-proceeding mechanism (Lesson 2) would be better as the opening rather than the second lesson, since it explains the failure the reader arrived with.

The three-question test for sorting negative boundaries in Lesson 5 (irreversible / visible to others / hides the work) is a synthesis. No source publishes it as a test. The first two questions map onto action classes Anthropic's prompting documentation groups explicitly, and the third is derived from the scope-expansion material plus the reviewability concern in the Claude Code failure-pattern list — but the grouping into three questions applied as a filter is authored structure. The lesson text says so in the sentence introducing it, which is honest, and a reader could still come away treating it as established practice.

The six-part brief structure (Goal, Context, Output, Criteria, Boundaries, When Stuck) is assembled rather than sourced as a unit. Four of the parts are OpenAI's published frame and are attributed as such in the lesson; Criteria is added from the GitHub and Anthropic harness material; When Stuck is authored, derived from the Ambig-SWE finding that the default is silence. The assembly is stated in the lesson as a combination with its sources named, but no vendor publishes this six-part shape and a reader may assume one does.

Every worked example and faded example is constructed, not captured from real runs. The agent exchange in Lesson 2 in particular reads more cleanly than a real interview does — four well-formed questions, no recoverable ones, no misunderstanding of the request. The lesson warns that question quality varies and cites the finding about wasted turns, but the demonstration itself models a best case, so a reader's first real interview will be messier than the example prepares them for.

The course teaches criteria and evidence without being able to guarantee the reader's tool returns either. Lesson 3's Level 2 exercise depends on the agent reporting command output and counts, and some surfaces summarize rather than transcribe. The exercise handles this by making 'unproven' a first-class verdict, which converts the gap into a finding rather than a dead end, but a reader on a tool that returns only prose summaries gets a weaker version of that exercise than the rubric implies.

The 74% figure in Lesson 2 is the one number in the course carrying real weight, and it is doing more work than a single benchmark result should. It is presented with its three conditions, its status as an upper bound, its variance across models, and the caveat that the simulated user was unrealistically cooperative — but it is still a single study, and no independent replication of that specific magnitude was found during sourcing.
followUpChecks: Re-verify the five undated documentation pages on the next pass. The Anthropic prompting best-practices page is organized around a named model list and the Opus 5 page describes one model's behaviour; both will be superseded, and Lesson 5's scope-expansion argument depends on the second.

Watch whether scope expansion and self-assessment leniency persist in newer model generations. Lesson 5 is built on the first and Lesson 3 on the second; if vendors stop reporting them, both lessons need rebuilding rather than patching, and Lesson 5's boundary section would shrink to the irreversible and visible-to-others classes.

Check whether Ambig-SWE's interaction gain has been re-measured on current models, or replicated elsewhere. If a newer figure exists, replace the number in Lesson 2 rather than the argument; if the effect narrows substantially on newer models, the lesson's cost/benefit framing for the interview step needs revisiting.

Capture one real agent interview transcript, including its weak questions, and consider replacing or supplementing Lesson 2's constructed exchange. That would close the gap between the demonstration's cleanliness and what a reader's first attempt returns.

When the sibling course verify-agent-output is written, check Lesson 3 against it for overlap. The seam between 'criteria written into a brief' and 'verification gates built around a project' is the most likely place in the ladder for duplication, and this course deliberately stops at the first.

acceptanceReview.rubricNotes: pedagogy 4 rather than 5: the worked-to-faded-to-independent ladder is present in all five lessons, but the faded examples in Lessons 1, 3, and 5 are fill-in-the-blank tables, which fade the content while leaving the structure fully given — the reader is always told how many slots there are and what each column means. Lesson 4's faded example is the strongest of the five because it asks the reader to audit their own answer for a property nobody named. load 4 rather than 5: Lesson 3 carries four new concepts (self-assessment leniency, checkable criteria, criteria-before-implementation, evidence-over-assertion) plus the literal-following caution and the process-versus-result distinction, which sits at the top of the intended band; it holds together because all six are facets of one question — how do you say what done means — but it is the densest lesson here and the one to split if the course is ever expanded.
acceptanceReview.terminalTask: In Lesson 5's Level 2 exercise the reader assembles the six-part brief they have been building since Lesson 1, runs it end to end with their own agent against their own real task, grades each acceptance criterion from the returned evidence before reading the summary, and traces every remaining gap to a named section of the brief. The artifact is a real brief file plus a graded run on their own machine, and the trace is what makes it repeatable: the reader finishes able to point at the sentence that failed rather than concluding the brief was vague.
acceptanceReview.interactionCheck: Four blocks across five lessons, none in an exercise region, none in Lesson 3's exercise-heavy tail. Lesson 1 uses agentmentor-check ('Separate recoverable from decision blanks') for the misconception that a better brief means a fuller one; all three wrong options are things a reader would genuinely be tempted to write down, and each feedback names why stating it costs more than it buys rather than just marking it wrong. Lesson 2 uses agentmentor-order ('Order the steps that produce an asked question') because the four steps have a real dependency — the interview instruction must precede the request, and readers reliably invert this by polishing the request first; feedbackWrong points at the dependency rather than at a position. Lesson 3 uses agentmentor-check ('Pick the criterion that closes the gap') for the misconception that a measurable criterion is a sufficient one; the three wrong options are a criterion that was already true before the fix, one satisfied by a proxy, and one satisfied by a confident wrong explanation, which are the three real ways a criterion goes hollow. Lesson 4 uses agentmentor-diff ('Read what the added examples changed') because the accidental-rule problem is only visible by comparing two example sets side by side — the shared property of a set is not a property of any single member, so no single-item block can pose it; focus directs attention to what each set shares without naming which set is better. Lesson 2 also carries the course's one agentmentor-action (confusion_breaker), which sends the reader's own unedited request to an agent under an instruction to name its assumptions without doing the work, and its rules include the load-bearing constraint that the agent must ask what the reader intended before offering its own default, since a suggested answer overwrites the one being tested. Lesson 5 deliberately uses no deterministic block: its judgment — which prohibitions earn a line — depends on the reader's own task and stakes, so any fixed correct answer would be arbitrary, and the three-question sort is exercised in the faded example and Level 1 exercise instead. No agentmentor-live anywhere: this course has no front-end visible effect, and simulating an agent run would be theatre rather than deterministic local feedback. No predict, trace, code, fix, or hotspot: there is no code here to predict, trace, complete, or fix, and no structure diagram with a single responsible node to click.
acceptanceReview.learnerFitCheck: Targets the reader who can delegate and keeps getting the wrong thing back. Known: running an agent, judging finished work in their own domain, opening files. Unknown: programming, formal specification writing, test frameworks, Skills, repo structure, prompt-engineering vocabulary, and benchmark methodology. Hidden prerequisites removed: acceptance criteria are taught entirely without test vocabulary, using counts, timings, diffs, and observable states — and the one worked criterion mentioning a test suite exists to show why that criterion is weak, so a reader who does not know what a test suite proves loses nothing. The two research papers are introduced through their findings, never their methods; the reader is not asked to interpret a benchmark, and the single numeric claim carries its experimental setting in the same paragraph so it can be read without knowing how such studies are run. Every worked example is drawn from mixed domains — invoices, onboarding emails, analytics events, a form, a payment flow — and the code that appears is short, illustrative, and never load-bearing for the argument. The first independent action is listing what one of the reader's own past requests failed to say and sorting each item with two yes/no questions; it needs a text editor and their memory of a run they already had, and depends on nothing in unknownConcepts. The first real run comes in Lesson 5, by which point the reader has decisions, criteria, examples, and boundaries written down, so the run they start is one they have fully specified.
acceptanceReview.citationCheck: Every [^Sn] sits under the sentence it supports, and every source was opened during this session on 2026-08-23. Load-bearing placements: Lesson 1's definition of underspecification quotes Ambig-SWE's own definitional sentence, and the 56.0% missing-information figure sits on the annotation study that produced it, with its sample described in the same sentence. Lesson 2's mechanism claim rests on the next-token-prediction sentence from the paper that states it, not on any general hallucination literature; the detection finding, the non-interactive default, and the 74% figure all sit on Ambig-SWE, and the number is surrounded by its three conditions and its variance rather than quoted bare. Lesson 3's central mechanism quotes the Claude Code documentation's own 'looks done' sentence, and the self-assessment finding quotes the harness post's direct observation of agents praising their own work — no adjacent-field calibration or overconfidence literature is reached for anywhere in this course. The criteria-before-implementation claim quotes the sprint-contract paragraph describing a practice that was actually run, not a recommendation. Lesson 4's example rules quote the prompting page's own three properties and its stated 3-5 count. Lesson 5's scope-expansion claim quotes the Opus 5 page's own sentence about that model and is stamped in prose as an as-of-2026-08-23 snapshot; the boundary-budget guidance quotes OpenAI's own two-sentence statement of it. No source is stretched past what its page says: the reasons-generalize principle is cited for what it claims about explanations and is not extended into a claim about compliance rates, and the three-question boundary test is explicitly labelled a synthesis in the lesson text rather than attributed to any source. Two candidate sources were dropped rather than cited from summaries: the OpenAI SWE-bench Verified announcement (403 on every attempt, so the annotation rubric behind Ambig-SWE's definition is cited only through the paper that uses it) and the Anthropic interactive prompt-engineering tutorial repository (reachable, but its teaching text was not readable at chapter level without opening notebooks, so it is recorded in the registry line only and backs no claim).
acceptanceReview.sourceRecheck: All ten sources were opened during this session on 2026-08-23, not reused from cache. Both papers were downloaded as PDFs and read as extracted text, so every figure quoted comes from the paper body rather than from an abstract or a summary. The five documentation pages were fetched as raw markdown via their .md endpoints after the standard HTML URLs region-redirected; the quoted text comes from those fetched bodies, and the canonical page URLs recorded in sources.md were separately confirmed to return 200. The Anthropic harness post was fetched and text-extracted in full, and its publication date read off the page. Publication dates are recorded where the page carries one; the five versioned pages are recorded as retrieved 2026-08-23 rather than given an invented date.
acceptanceReview.ambigSweFigureNote: The 74% figure was resolved from the paper PDF, not from secondary coverage. It appears in the v3 abstract (revised 2026-02-21) and again in the introduction with its setting: 'interactivity can boost performance on underspecified inputs by up to 74% over the non-interactive settings, though performance varies across models'. The comparison is Interaction versus Hidden across the 500 issues of SWE-Bench Verified, where Hidden is a GPT-4o-summarized underspecified issue with interaction disabled and Interaction is the same summarized issue with a GPT-4o user proxy holding the full issue and interaction made compulsory by prompt. Lesson 2 states the number, the three conditions, its status as the largest gain among the models tested, its variance, and the cooperative-proxy caveat, and directs the reader to take the direction rather than the magnitude.
promotionNotes: Slug is final and descriptive; no temporary showcase, test, or dogfood naming anywhere in the course.

Before promoting to examples, re-verify the five undated documentation pages per followUpChecks. Lesson 5's argument depends on a model-specific behaviour that is stamped with its date in prose but will need re-checking rather than re-writing if it persists.

The constructed agent interview in Lesson 2 would be stronger as a real transcript including its weak questions; that is a quality improvement rather than a correctness fix and is recorded as a weak point rather than a blocker.

Translation note for sibling locales: several glossary keys are English phrases that appear verbatim mid-sentence in the prose by design — 'WHEN STUCK', 'Boundaries', 'Instructions Missing Key Information', 'how much work is authorized', 'trust-then-verify gap', 'process criteria', 'non-interactive behavior'. Each must appear verbatim in the translated body or the hover card detaches; the first three are proper names of sections or categories and should stay in English with a translated gloss.

nextSteps: Have a human review the outline before relying on this course: it was auto-confirmed in a non-interactive run, and nobody checked whether five lessons in this order is the right decomposition. If the order or coverage is off, revise before translating.
Read Lesson 1 and run one of your own failed requests through the two-question filter before going further.
Do Lesson 2's action card on a request you are about to send, and note which of its assumptions would have been wrong.
Assemble the six-part brief in Lesson 5 and run it on a real task, then trace each remaining gap to the section responsible — that trace, not the template, is what makes the next brief better.
